objectives: Identify quotients and remainders upon the division of polynomials.
Apply the Remainder Theorem and the Factor Theorem.
Use synthetic division to divide a polynomial by a linear polynomial with leading coefficient 1.

standards.text: Know and apply the Remainder Theorem: For a polynomial p(x) and a number a, the remainder on division by x - a is p(a), so p(a) = 0 if and only if (x - a) is a factor of p(x).

Rewrite simple rational expressions in different forms; write a(x)/b(x) in the form q(x) + r(x)/b(x), where a(x), b(x), q(x), and r(x) are polynomials with the degree of r(x) less than the degree of b(x), using inspection, long division, or, for the more complicated examples, a computer algebra system.
Use the structure of an expression to identify ways to rewrite it.

recap: Dividing a polynomial by x − a gives a quotient and a remainder, the remainder equals p(a), and a zero remainder means x − a is a factor.

diagnose.doneWhen: All three answers are written without a calculator, and you can say how Question 3 and Question 2 are alike.
diagnose.notes: Answers. Q1: 4 − 6 + 5 = 3. Q2: x² + 5x + 6 + 1 = x² + 5x + 7. Q3: 17 = 3 × 5 + 2, quotient 3, remainder 2. Q2 and Q3 are alike: dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder, the idea behind polynomial division. Verbal misconceptions: Q1 students square −3x as 9x or compute 2² as 4 and then 4 − 3 + 5 slip to 6; Q2 students forget to add the 1 or write 5x² ; Q3 students write 3.4 and do not give a remainder. Adaptive routing: if >30% miss Q1, rehearse substitution with brackets before slide 7; if >30% miss Q2, expand with a grid before slide 5; if >30% miss Q3, write 17 = 5 × 3 + 2 and go to slide 5. If all three are secure, move quickly through slide 5 and start the Investigate route early.

blocks.title: Quotient and remainder
blocks.notes: Worked solutions (HSA.APR.D.6). Polynomial division mirrors 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2: the DIVIDEND equals the DIVISOR times the QUOTIENT plus the REMAINDER, and the remainder has smaller degree than the divisor. Long division: Example A: x² ÷ x = x, so the first quotient term is x; x(x + 2) = x² + 2x; subtract: 3x + 7; 3x ÷ x = 3; 3(x + 2) = 3x + 6; subtract: 1. Quotient x + 3, remainder 1. Check: (x + 2)(x + 3) + 1 = x² + 5x + 6 + 1 ✓. Example B: 2x² ÷ x = 2x; 2x(x − 4) = 2x² − 8x; subtract: 5x − 5; 5x ÷ x = 5; 5(x − 4) = 5x − 20; subtract: 15. Quotient 2x + 5, remainder 15. Check: 2x² − 8x + 5x − 20 + 15 = 2x² − 3x − 5 ✓. In rational form (a proper rational function has remainder degree less than the divisor degree): (x² + 5x + 7)/(x + 2) = x + 3 + 1/(x + 2). Verbal misconceptions: subtracting only the first term of each product (sign errors in the second term, −8x subtracted as +8x); leaving a remainder of the same degree as the divisor; forgetting to write the remainder over the divisor. Adaptive routing: if >30% slip on the subtraction, write the subtraction as 'change every sign' and redo Example B; if >30% forget the remainder, link to 17 = 3 × 5 + 2. Gate Q2 routes to slide 5 or 6.

blocks.title: Synthetic division
blocks.notes: Worked solutions (HSA.APR.B.2 and D.6). Synthetic division is a shortcut for dividing by a LINEAR divisor x − a with leading coefficient 1. Write a in the box (the opposite sign to the constant in the divisor) and the coefficients of the dividend, including zeros for missing powers. Bring down the first coefficient; multiply by a and add to the next; repeat. The last number is the remainder and the others are the quotient coefficients, one degree lower. Example A: box 1; coefficients 1, 3, −4, −5. Bring down 1; 1 × 1 = 1, 3 + 1 = 4; 4 × 1 = 4, −4 + 4 = 0; 0 × 1 = 0, −5 + 0 = −5. Quotient x² + 4x + 0, remainder −5. Check at x = 2: p(2) = 8 + 12 − 8 − 5 = 7 and (2 − 1)(4 + 8) − 5 = 7 ✓. Example B: divisor x + 1, so the box is −1. Coefficients 2, −5, 1, 6. Bring down 2; 2 × (−1) = −2, −5 − 2 = −7; −7 × (−1) = 7, 1 + 7 = 8; 8 × (−1) = −8, 6 − 8 = −2. Quotient 2x² − 7x + 8, remainder −2. Verbal misconceptions: using +1 instead of −1 for x + 1; omitting the zero for a missing power; reading the last number as part of the quotient; trying it for 2x − 3 (leading coefficient not 1). Adaptive routing: if >30% use the wrong sign in the box, write 'x − a, so the box holds a' and redo Example B; if >30% skip the zero, show x³ − 7x + 6 with 0x². Gate Q1 routes to this slide.

blocks.title: The Remainder Theorem
blocks.whatif: What if the divisor is x − 3 and p(x) = x³ − 7x + 6? Predict the remainder from p(3), then check by synthetic division.
blocks.notes: Worked solutions (HSA.APR.B.2). Why it works: if p(x) = (x − a)q(x) + r, then substituting x = a makes the first term zero and leaves p(a) = r. So the remainder is found by substitution, with no division. Example A: p(3) = 27 − 36 + 3 + 9 = 3. Check by synthetic division, box 3: 1, −4 + 3 = −1, 1 − 3 = −2, 9 − 6 = 3 ✓. Example B: divisor x + 2 = x − (−2), so a = −2: p(−2) = 2(−8) + 5(4) − 3(−2) + 1 = −16 + 20 + 6 + 1 = 11. Check, box −2: 2, 5 − 4 = 1, −3 − 2 = −5, 1 + 10 = 11 ✓. What if (gold strip): p(3) = 27 − 21 + 6 = 12; synthetic division, box 3, coefficients 1, 0, −7, 6: 1, 3, 2, 12 ✓, so the remainder is 12. Verbal misconceptions: evaluating p(−3) for the divisor x − 3 (opposite sign); evaluating p(a) but calling it the quotient; arithmetic slips with negative cubes. Adaptive routing: if >30% use the wrong sign, ask 'what makes the divisor zero?' and redo Example B; if >30% slip with (−2)³, show (−2)³ = −8 in brackets. Gate Q2 routes to this slide.

blocks.title: The Factor Theorem
blocks.whatif: What if x + 4 is tested on the same cubic? Predict p(−4) before you substitute, then use it to confirm the factorisation.
blocks.notes: Worked solutions (HSA.APR.B.2). FACTOR THEOREM: p(a) = 0 exactly when x − a is a factor. Example A: try small integer values: p(−1) = −1 + 2 + 11 − 12 = 0, so x + 1 is a factor. Synthetic division with box −1: 1; 2 − 1 = 1; −11 − 1 = −12; −12 + 12 = 0. Quotient x² + x − 12 = (x + 4)(x − 3). So p(x) = (x + 1)(x + 4)(x − 3). Check p(3) = 27 + 18 − 33 − 12 = 0 ✓ and p(−4) = −64 + 32 + 44 − 12 = 0 ✓. Example B: p(2) = 8 + 4k − 2 − 10 = 4k − 4 = 0, so k = 1. Check: x³ + x² − x − 10 at x = 2 is 8 + 4 − 2 − 10 = 0 ✓. What if (gold strip): p(−4) = 0 as computed, which confirms that x + 4 is a factor. Verbal misconceptions: testing p(1) for the factor x + 1; stopping after finding one factor and not factoring the quotient; believing a non-zero remainder means 'no solutions'. Adaptive routing: if >30% test the wrong sign, repeat 'what number makes the factor zero?'; if >30% stop at the quadratic, ask them to factor it. Gate Q3 routes to this slide.

practice.done: Done when: the box number has the opposite sign to the constant in the divisor, the last number is read as the remainder, and the answer is checked by substituting.

apply.done: Done when: the divisor is written as x − a first, the Remainder Theorem is used when only a remainder is needed, and each answer is checked.

investigate.done: Done when: your argument uses p(a) or the form p(x) = (x − a)q(x) + r, and the explanation says why it holds for every n.

practice.notes: Answers. Practice 1: box 2, coefficients 1, −4, 5, −2: 1, −2, 1, 0 gives x² − 2x + 1, remainder 0 (so x − 2 is a factor). Practice 2: p(2) = 8 + 2 − 9 = 1. Apply 1 (a model freight crate for a Jeddah rail terminal, model values): box −1, coefficients 1, 7, 14, 8: 1, 6, 8, 0; the base area is x² + 6x + 8 = (x + 2)(x + 4); check: (x + 1)(x² + 6x + 8) = x³ + 7x² + 14x + 8 ✓. Apply 2: p(−1) = −1 + k + 4 − 6 = k − 3 = 0, so k = 3. Investigate 1: put x = 1 in x^n − 1: 1 − 1 = 0, so by the Factor Theorem x − 1 is a factor for every n; for n = 3 the quotient is x² + x + 1. Investigate 2: x + 1 = x − (−1), so a = −1 and the remainder is p(−1) = 1 − 1 + 1 = 1 (since (−1)^50 = 1). Verbal misconceptions: Practice 1 using −2 in the box; Practice 2 computing p(−2); Apply 1 forgetting the final 0 means no remainder; Apply 2 substituting x = 1; Investigate 2 saying (−1)^50 = −1. Adaptive routing: if >30% miss Practice 1, route to slide 6; Practice 2, slide 7; Apply 1, slide 6; Apply 2, slide 8; Investigate, slide 7 or 8. Students who finish Apply early move to Investigate.

compare.title: Which route? Judge the claim

routes.name: SYNTHETIC DIVISION
routes.pro: Short and tidy for x − a.
routes.con: Only for a linear divisor with leading 1.

routes.name: REMAINDER THEOREM
routes.pro: Tests a factor in one line.
routes.con: Gives the remainder only, not the quotient.

compare.claim: Dividing by x − 3 and by x + 3 always gives the same remainder.
compare.assume: Did you test more than one polynomial and both signs of a?

spot.title: steal this shortcut
spot.text: To test a possible factor, substitute first. If p(a) is not zero you have just found the remainder, so no division is wasted.

compare.whatif: What if the remainder is 0? Predict what that tells you about the graph of p, then check with p(x) = x³ + x² − 14x − 24 at x = 4.
compare.notes: Compare and judge (3 min). Worked solutions. Divide p(x) = x³ + x² − 14x − 24 by x − 4. Long division: x³ ÷ x = x²; x²(x − 4) = x³ − 4x²; subtract: 5x² − 14x; 5x² ÷ x = 5x; 5x(x − 4) = 5x² − 20x; subtract: 6x − 24; 6(x − 4) = 6x − 24; remainder 0. Quotient x² + 5x + 6. Synthetic: box 4: 1, 5, 6, 0. Remainder Theorem: p(4) = 64 + 16 − 56 − 24 = 0, so x − 4 is a factor, and (x − 4)(x + 2)(x + 3) is the full factorisation. Claim: FALSE. Take p(x) = x² + x: p(3) = 12 and p(−3) = 6, different remainders. (It holds for an even polynomial such as x², which is the trap.) What if (gold box): a zero remainder means p(4) = 0, so the graph crosses the x-axis at x = 4. Verbal misconceptions: 'x − 3 and x + 3 are the same factor'; 'a remainder of zero means no quotient'; 'synthetic division always works'. Adaptive routing: if >30% mark the claim TRUE, have them compute p(3) and p(−3) for x² + x; if teams finish early, ask which route they would choose for 2x − 3 as a divisor and why.

production.title: Freight crate for the rail terminal
production.context: A model freight crate for a Haramain rail terminal in Jeddah (model values only, not real data) has volume V(x) = x³ + 9x² + 26x + 24 cubic metres. Its height is (x + 2) m, and the base is a rectangle.
tasks: Use synthetic division to find the base area, and factor it into the two sides of the base.
Find the three dimensions when x = 3 and check the volume.
A second crate has volume x³ + 9x² + 26x + 30 with the same height (x + 2). Find the remainder and say what it means.
doneWhen: The box number is −2 and the base area is x² + 7x + 12.
The base factors as (x + 3)(x + 4) and the dimensions at x = 3 are 5, 6 and 7 m.
The volume 210 m³ is checked as 5 × 6 × 7.
The remainder 6 is found with p(−2) and is explained as a non-exact fit.
production.hint: Hint for solving: the divisor x + 2 is x − (−2), so the box holds −2.
production.whatif: What if the height is (x + 3) for the first crate? Predict whether it is also a fit, using p(−3), then find the base area.
production.notes: Model values only, not real data. Task 1: box −2, coefficients 1, 9, 26, 24: 1; 9 − 2 = 7; 26 − 14 = 12; 24 − 24 = 0. Base area x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4). Task 2: at x = 3 the height is 5, the base sides are 6 and 7, so the volume is 5 × 6 × 7 = 210 m³; check V(3) = 27 + 81 + 78 + 24 = 210 ✓. Task 3: p(−2) = −8 + 36 − 52 + 30 = 6, so the remainder is 6 and the height x + 2 is NOT a factor: the volume is not exactly height × base, there is 6 m³ left over. What if (gold box): p(−3) = −27 + 81 − 78 + 24 = 0, so x + 3 is also a factor; box −3: 1, 6, 8, 0, base area x² + 6x + 8 = (x + 2)(x + 4); the three factors are x + 2, x + 3, x + 4. Verbal misconceptions: using +2 in the box; forgetting that a remainder of zero is needed for an exact fit; answering Task 2 with 3, 4 and 5 (confusing x and the dimensions). Adaptive routing: if >30% cannot start Task 1, return to slide 6 Example B; if >30% miss Task 3, slide 7; if >30% miss the factorisation, slide 8. Early finishers: show that x + 4 is also a factor of V(x).

gate.notes: Answers. Q1: box 3, coefficients 1, −6, 11, −6: 1, −3, 2, 0; quotient x² − 3x + 2 and remainder 0 (so x − 3 is a factor). Q2: p(−3) = −27 + 27 + 3 + 5 = 8. Q3: p(−1) = −1 + k + 4 − 6 = k − 3 = 0, so k = 3. Verbal misconceptions: Q1 using −3 in the box, or reading the 0 as part of the quotient; Q2 evaluating p(3) = 27 + 27 − 3 + 5 = 56; Q3 substituting x = 1. Adaptive routing: Q1 missed, route to slide 6; Q2 missed, slide 7; Q3 missed, slide 8. If a student misses two or more, they join the teacher group for the Smart Production create step; students who get all three correct start the create step immediately.

create: Choose a quadratic with two integer zeros and multiply by one more factor to build a cubic p(x).
Use the Factor Theorem to show one of your factors, and divide to check the quotient.
Swap with a partner and check their work. Then add a What if...? question (change one coefficient) and test your prediction.
smart.createDone: Done when: your cubic expands correctly, the Factor Theorem check and the division agree, and your What if...? question has a prediction and a test.
smart.exitIntro: Exit ticket: write your answer on a sticky note and place it on the door.
smart.next: Next lesson: more on zeros of polynomial functions.
smart.notes: Exit ticket solutions. Exit 1: p(3) = 27 − 6 + 5 = 26. Exit 2: p(−2) = −8 + 4 + 8 − 4 = 0, so yes, x + 2 is a factor; the quotient (box −2: 1, −1, −2, 0) is x² − x − 2 = (x − 2)(x + 1). Create step example: (x − 1)(x + 3) = x² + 2x − 3; times (x − 2): x³ − 7x + 6; p(1) = 0 ✓, box 1: 1, 1, −6, 0, quotient x² + x − 6 = (x − 2)(x + 3) ✓. What if: changing the constant to 7 gives p(1) = 1, so x − 1 is no longer a factor and the remainder is 1. Verbal misconceptions: Exit 1 using p(−3); Exit 2 stopping at p(−2) = 0 without answering 'yes'. Adaptive routing: if >30% miss Exit 1, retrieve slide 7 Example A; if >30% miss Exit 2, retrieve slide 8 Example A.

exam.notes: SAT (Advanced Math, polynomial factors): x − 3 a factor means p(3) = 0. p(3) = 2(27) − 5(9) − 3k + 3 = 54 − 45 + 3 − 3k = 12 − 3k = 0, so k = 4. Traps: using x = −3 (which gives a different k), forgetting the + 3, or answering 12. A student-produced-response grid answer is 4. GAT/Qudurat quantitative comparison (A is greater / B is greater / equal / cannot be determined): the remainder is p(2) = 5, which is more than 4, so A is greater. Trap: dividing 5 by something or using p(−2) = 5 (here equal by symmetry, which still gives A greater). SAAT/Tahsili (four options, for example A 3, B 5, C −3, D 7): divisor x + 1 gives a = −1; p(−1) = −2 + 1 + 4 = 3: A. Trap: p(1) = 5. Adaptive routing: if >30% miss the SAT item, return to slide 8 Example B; the GAT item, slide 7 Example A; the SAAT item, slide 7 Example B.
